Note that `current_user(request)` is called on line 11 and the resulting `user` is never used again, which strongly suggests the ownership check was intended and dropped. Add the check the sibling read handler already performs:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Missing `billing_name` in body raises KeyError

findings.title: No test exists for update_payment_method
findings.body: The new function update_payment_method is added with no test in this diff. It fetches a PaymentMethod, mutates it based on request body, and saves it — but nothing verifies it works correctly, that the returned dict reflects the update, or that ownership is enforced (the sibling read handler at lines 5-7 calls require_owner, but this function never does). Since the get_payment_method handler above appears to be tested per repository convention (it calls require_owner and current_user consistently), the same standard should apply here: a test asserting the update actually persists and that a non-owner request is rejected.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint loses its rate limit, enabling email flooding
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point whose `email` argument comes straight from the request and flows into `send_reset_email(email)` with no limiter in front of it any more. Adversary: any anonymous remote caller. What they control: the target address and the request rate. What they get: (a) an unbounded flood of reset mail into a victim's inbox, a well-known harassment/account-lockout-prep vector, (b) cheap high-volume probing of which addresses exist if the response or timing differs, and (c) burned sending quota and sender reputation for the whole product.

The PR's justification does not hold: a provider-side throttle is per-sending-account, not per-recipient and not per-source-IP. It caps your bill, not the victim's inbox, and once it engages it degrades reset mail for every legitimate user — the throttle becomes the denial of service rather than the defence.

Restore a limiter here. If the 5/hour bucket was too tight in practice, widen it or key it per-email-plus-IP rather than removing it, and keep the response constant regardless of whether the address exists.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Password reset endpoint now has no per-caller bound on sends

findings.title: No test guards the removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The decorator enforcing '5/hour' on request_reset was deleted, but no test file is included in this diff. If this change is wrong (e.g., the email provider does not actually throttle, or does so insufficiently), nothing would fail — there is no test asserting request_reset is rate-limited or exercising repeated calls to confirm expected throttling behaviour is preserved elsewhere.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
`read_export` resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it (line 14). `read_export_preview` instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` (line 20). `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Since the PR description says the preview path reuses the same layout as download, the omission looks unintentional. Route line 20 through `_confined(name)` exactly as line 14 does, so both entry points share one containment check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: preview skips _confined() used by download

findings.title: New preview function has no test covering its path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above which calls _confined(name). No test in this diff exercises read_export_preview, so a regression (e.g. reintroducing or failing to add confinement, or an off-by-one in the limit truncation) would go undetected. Add a test asserting that a traversal-style name is rejected/confined and that the returned bytes are truncated to `limit`.

findings.title: PR description says preview 'reuses same layout' but code diverges
findings.body: The PR summary states 'Preview path reuses the same layout as download,' implying read_export_preview follows the same pattern as the existing download function (which calls _confined(name) at line 14). Instead, read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, skipping the _confined helper entirely. A reviewer trusting the description would believe the same safety/behavioral guarantees apply to both functions, which is not the case as written.

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export leaks other tenants' reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes `report_ids` from the request, loads each `Report` by id, and now serialises them with `to_dict()` without any authorisation check. The `require_owner(user, report)` loop — which `api/auth.py` documents as mandatory for "every object read or mutation of another tenant's data" — was deleted along with its import.

Adversary: any authenticated user (any tenant). What they control: the `report_ids` list. What they get: the full contents of arbitrary reports belonging to other tenants, simply by enumerating or guessing ids. Authentication via `current_user` is still performed, but authentication is not authorisation — `user` is now computed on line 5 and never used.

If the loop is the performance problem, keep the check and make it a bulk one, e.g. filter the query by `tenant_id` at load time (`Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) or retain `require_owner` over the fetched set. Do not ship the endpoint with no check at all.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership

findings.title: No test exists to catch removal of tenant ownership check in bulk_export
findings.body: bulk_export previously enforced require_owner(user, report) for each report, ensuring cross-tenant reports could not be exported. That check was removed and nothing in the diff shows a test that calls bulk_export with report_ids belonging to another tenant and asserts a Forbidden error or empty/filtered result. If this change is wrong, a test exercising cross-tenant access would be the only thing to catch it, and no such test is present.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the driver never escapes them. The PR describes this as a support-facing name/status search, meaning the values originate from a request. Anyone who can reach that search can submit a `term` such as `%' UNION SELECT ... -- ` to read arbitrary tables, or `'; DROP TABLE customers; -- ` depending on driver multi-statement behaviour, and `status` is equally exposed.

Fix by keeping the wildcards in the parameter value rather than the SQL text, matching the sibling `get_customer`:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ LIKE wildcards in `term` are not escaped

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract and breaks on apostrophes
findings.body: `execute` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value.", and the existing `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)`. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is plainly wrong for reachable, non-malicious input: a support agent searching for `O'Brien` produces `... name LIKE '%O'Brien%' ...`, which is a syntax error and raises at the driver. Likewise a `None` status renders the literal string `'None'` and silently matches nothing rather than meaning "any status". Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))` so the driver quotes the values.

findings.title: search_customers has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds SQL via f-string interpolation and calls execute without params, bypassing the parameterised pattern used by get_customer. There is no test in this diff exercising it, so a broken query, wrong filter logic, or the injection risk itself would not be caught by any test run.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces
findings.body:
The existing send path parses the URL and rejects anything whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before issuing the request on line 10. `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no equivalent check, so a tenant-registered value reaches the HTTP client unvalidated \u2014 including internal hosts, loopback, and cloud metadata addresses. Since the response `status_code` is returned to the caller, the result is also an observable signal about internal services.

Apply the same host resolution and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` membership check here before the request, ideally by factoring lines 8-9 into a shared validator both functions call. Note that even with the check added, `requests` follows redirects by default, so a permitted host can 302 to an internal one; pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop) to make the check hold.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check and enables SSRF

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a GET to an arbitrary URL with no host allow-list check (unlike the existing post-based function above it), and there is no test file in this diff exercising it. A test asserting it rejects disallowed hosts, or even a basic happy-path test, would catch a regression or the missing validation; right now nothing would fail if this function were wrong.

findings.title: verify_endpoint's name implies a boolean result but it returns an int
findings.body: `verify_endpoint(url)` returns `requests.get(url, timeout=5).status_code`, an integer HTTP status code, not a pass/fail verification result. A caller reading the name would reasonably expect a boolean (or exception) indicating whether the endpoint is valid/reachable, and could misuse the return value (e.g. `if verify_endpoint(url):` succeeds for any non-zero status, including 404 or 500). A short docstring or a rename (e.g. `get_endpoint_status`) would remove the ambiguity.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` on a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices`. The Public Access Block is the last-resort guardrail that makes a public ACL or bucket policy a no-op; switching it off means any subsequent `public-read` ACL on an uploaded object, any overly broad bucket policy, or any principal with `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutObjectAcl` can expose customer invoices to anonymous internet readers, and nothing in the infrastructure will stop it.

Adversary: any unauthenticated internet user once a public ACL/policy exists, or any internal principal (or compromised CI role) with ACL/policy write permissions who can create one. What they control: the object ACL or bucket policy. What they get: read access to customer billing documents — names, addresses, amounts, likely tax IDs.

Fix: either omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` for `invoices` (the AWS default for new buckets is all-blocked) or set all four attributes to `true`. Public exposure should never be the default for this data class; if a specific object must be shared, use a presigned URL or CloudFront with OAC rather than disabling the guardrail bucket-wide.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled

findings.title: Undisclosed resource: PR says 'public assets bucket', adds an invoices bucket
findings.body:
The PR description says only "Public assets bucket for the marketing site, next to the existing private one", but the only genuinely new resources in this diff are `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` and its Public Access Block — the assets block at lines 6–11 is an unchanged/reformatted existing resource. A security-relevant resource that is not mentioned in the change description will not get the review it needs.

Please confirm this bucket is intended here (rather than a copy-paste from another module) and, if it is, split it out or describe it, including who is expected to read from it.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same kind of HMAC digest as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. String `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a signature to be recovered byte-by-byte and arbitrary webhook payloads to be accepted as authentic. The function immediately above (line 7) already does this correctly. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test exercises verify_acmepay's comparison behavior
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new and untested. Nothing in this diff would fail if the function's comparison logic were wrong (e.g. returning the wrong boolean, or using == vs hmac.compare_digest). Since no test file is included in the diff, add a test verifying verify_acmepay returns True for a valid signature and False for an invalid one, mirroring whatever coverage verify_stripe has.

findings.title: Full traceback and exception text returned to HTTP clients on 500
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response body that is sent back with the 500 status. Anyone who can reach the endpoint — including unauthenticated callers, since a 500 handler runs for failures that occur before or independently of auth — can provoke an error (malformed input, oversized field, unexpected type) and read back internal file paths, the deployment directory layout, module and dependency names/versions, and the source line that failed. Exception messages are frequently worse than the stack itself: database drivers embed the failing SQL and sometimes the DSN, HTTP clients embed internal URLs and hostnames, and `KeyError`/decode errors embed fragments of configuration. That output is exactly the reconnaissance an attacker needs to aim a follow-up (SQLi probing, SSRF against a now-known internal host, path traversal against a now-known layout).

The stated goal — on-call seeing what failed without SSHing in — is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8. Keep the client-facing body opaque and correlate via an identifier instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    request_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"request_id": request_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": request_id}, 500
```

If verbose bodies are genuinely wanted for local work, gate them on an explicit debug setting that is off by default in production rather than emitting them unconditionally.

Separately: `traceback.format_exc()` reads the *currently handled* exception from thread state. If `handle` is ever called outside an `except` block (e.g. a framework passes the exception object along after the handler frame has unwound), this yields the string `"NoneType: None"` rather than the trace for `exc`, so the feature does not reliably deliver what it promises even ignoring the disclosure.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores `exc` and yields "NoneType: None" outside a handler

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape changed: new key and non-constant `error` value

findings.title: No test verifies the response contents of handle()
findings.body: The change alters what handle() returns on error (now including exception message and full traceback in the response body). There is no test in this diff asserting the shape or content of this return value, so a future change to this function (e.g., reverting the leak, or introducing a further regression) would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Password reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` runs the raw password through a single unsalted MD5, which is a fast, GPU-friendly, collision-broken hash with ubiquitous precomputed rainbow tables. The adversary is anyone who obtains the stored reset hashes \u2014 via SQL injection elsewhere, a backup leak, a read-only DB replica, or an insider. They control nothing; they simply look the digests up or brute force them at billions of guesses per second, and they get the users' plaintext passwords, which are then reusable against this service and any other where the user reused them.

There is no reason for a second scheme here: line 7 already uses bcrypt with a per-password salt. Make this function call the same primitive, e.g. `return hash_password(raw)` / `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode()`, and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw`. If the intent was a short-lived reset *token* rather than a password, it still should not be MD5 \u2014 generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and store a SHA-256 of the token, comparing with `hmac.compare_digest`.

Any hashes already written by this function must be treated as compromised and forced to re-hash on next login.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with the existing bcrypt hash
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-character MD5 hex digest. If both values land in the same stored column and are verified through `bcrypt.checkpw`, the MD5 value is not a valid bcrypt salt/hash and `checkpw` will raise `ValueError: invalid salt` (or simply never match), so a user who went through the reset path can no longer log in. There is also no companion verify function for the MD5 form in the diff, so it is unclear how a caller is expected to check it. Either produce the reset hash with `bcrypt.hashpw` as well (keeping one storage format and one verification path), or add an explicit algorithm discriminator plus a matching verify helper.

findings.title: No test coverage for hash_reset_password
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new function used for password reset hashing, but no test file is present in this diff. There is nothing that would fail if this function's behavior changed (e.g., algorithm swapped, output format changed, or reverted to a stronger hash). Since this function handles security-sensitive password material, its behavior should be pinned down with a test.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs forked PR code with NPM_TOKEN in env
findings.body:
This change creates a "pwn request". `pull_request_target` (line 4) runs the workflow in the context of the base repository, so it has access to repository secrets and a privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and unlike `pull_request` it triggers for pull requests from forks **without maintainer approval**. Lines 11-12 then explicitly check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` exported into its environment (lines 14-15).

Attacker: any GitHub user who can open a pull request. What they control: the entire contents of the checked-out tree, including `scripts/measure.sh` itself (and anything it sources, plus `package.json` lifecycle scripts, lockfile-resolved dependencies, etc.). What they get: the plaintext `NPM_TOKEN` (curl it to a server they control, or just print it obfuscated in logs), plus whatever the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` scopes allow — with no `permissions:` block declared, that may include `contents: write`, i.e. pushing to the base repository. No victim interaction and no second request is needed; opening the PR is the whole exploit.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. Forked PRs do get this signal under `pull_request`; what they do not get is access to secrets. If the only reason for the switch was secret access, that is exactly the thing that must not be granted.
2. If `pull_request_target` is genuinely required, never check out or execute the PR head under it. Keep the checkout at the base ref and compute the diff size from the API / `git fetch` of the head without running any code from it.
3. Split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that runs the untrusted script and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact and holds the secret.

In any case, drop `NPM_TOKEN` from a job that executes PR-controlled code, add an explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block, and rotate `NPM_TOKEN` if this workflow has already run on any external PR.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + head checkout runs fork code with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: pull_request_target does not achieve the stated goal
findings.body:
The PR description says the change exists so external contributors get the same CI signal. `pull_request` already triggers for pull requests from forks — the difference is only that fork runs get a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and no secrets. So if the size check was not running for forks before, the cause was something else (for example a branch/path filter, a required-secret failure, or the `fork` runs being skipped by repo settings), and switching the trigger addresses a symptom rather than the cause.

Additionally, under `pull_request_target` the workflow *definition* is always read from the base branch, so future edits to `size.yml` in a PR will not be exercised by that PR's own run — a behaviour change worth being deliberate about.

findings.title: Digest key rejects contexts the old tuple key accepted
findings.body: The old key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` worked for any context whose keys were mutually comparable and whose values were hashable — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `frozenset`, or any object with `__hash__` were all fine. `json.dumps` accepts a strictly smaller set: anything outside dict/list/str/int/float/bool/None raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable`, and the exception escapes `cached_render` before `_render` is ever called. Callers that previously rendered successfully with e.g. a `datetime` in the context will now fail outright. If the digest form is wanted, pass a `default=repr`-style fallback to `json.dumps` (accepting the collision caveat) or fall back to the previous tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: New JSON-based key requires JSON-serializable context; untested
findings.body: The key derivation changed from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` to `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`. This restricts context values to JSON-serializable types (no sets, datetimes, custom objects, etc.) whereas the old tuple-based approach tolerated a broader range of hashable values. None of the added tests exercise a context with a non-JSON-serializable value, so a regression that breaks previously-working callers (e.g. passing a set or object as a context value) would not be caught.

findings.title: Test only asserts shell=False, not that args are a safe list
findings.body:
test_runs_without_a_shell only checks `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`. It never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (or equivalent) to confirm that `name` and `directory` are passed as separate list elements rather than being reassembled into a single interpolated string. The entire point of this PR is switching from a shell string to argv list; a future refactor that keeps shell=False but reintroduces string interpolation (e.g. `["sh", "-c", f"tar -czf ... {directory}"]`) would still pass this test.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `spy` fixture is not defined in this change

findings.title: `directory` is now a single argv element, not shell-split
findings.body:
Under the old `shell=True` form, `directory` was interpolated into a command string and then word-split and glob-expanded by the shell, so callers could legitimately pass `"/srv/a /srv/b"` or `"/srv/data/*"` and tar would receive several operands. With the list form the whole string becomes one literal path operand, so those calls now fail with `tar: /srv/a /srv/b: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and `check=True` turns that into a `CalledProcessError` at runtime rather than a test failure.

If multi-path/glob callers exist, change the signature to accept a sequence of directories (`*directories` or a list) and splat it after `--`. If they do not, that is worth confirming against the call sites before merge, since nothing in this diff proves it.

Related, smaller: `{1,64}` with `fullmatch` now rejects any previously working name longer than 64 characters, and any name containing `.` or spaces, with a `ValueError` where the old code would have produced an archive.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, but `directory` is passed straight into the argv on line 12 with no check. Because argv is a list and `--` terminates option parsing, this is no longer a command-injection or argument-injection sink — the worst case is that tar archives whatever path is supplied. If `directory` originates from a request parameter or job payload anywhere upstream, a caller could pass `/etc` or `/root` and then retrieve `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` for an arbitrary-file-read. If every caller supplies a server-derived path, there is nothing to do here.

Suggested follow-up: resolve `directory` with `os.path.realpath` and assert it is inside the expected export root before invoking tar, mirroring the allowlist discipline already applied to `name`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and then ends. The test passes for any return value — empty string, `None`, garbage, or a partially rendered header — as long as `render` does not raise. That makes it a smoke test masquerading as a behavioural one, and a regression that silently changes the blank-invoice output will not be caught.

Assert the expected output explicitly, e.g. `assert render(Invoice(lines=[])) == "<expected blank output>"`, or at minimum assert on the specific property the empty case is supposed to guarantee (no line-item section, totals still present).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Mock-only assertion never checks rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only asserts fmt.call_count == 2. It never checks the actual rendered string produced by render(). If format_line's output is wrong, dropped, or mis-ordered in the final render, this test still passes as long as it's called twice. Assert on the actual rendered content (e.g., that render() includes the formatted line items) instead of, or in addition to, the mock call count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test verifies the mock, not the rendered output

findings.title: Failing test deleted with no implementation fix and no replacement
findings.body:
The PR description says the rounding was fixed and the stale test dropped, but this diff touches only `tests/test_rounding.py` and contains only deletions — there is no change to `round_cents` anywhere in the change set. Either the implementation fix is missing from this PR, or the behaviour was never changed and a genuinely failing assertion was removed to make the suite green.

Either way, the half-to-even boundary (`Decimal("2.345")`) is now completely untested: no replacement test asserting the new expected value was added. If the intended behaviour is now half-up, add `assert round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")` rather than deleting the case, so the boundary stays pinned.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding fix has no test covering the corrected behaviour

findings.title: `Decimal` import may now be unused depending on remaining tests
findings.body: `from decimal import Decimal` on line 1 was used by the deleted test. The remaining `test_rounds_up_above_half` is not shown in full, so it may or may not still use `Decimal`. If it does not, this import is now dead and lint will flag it. Worth a quick check while removing the test.

findings.title: Patch targets notify.transport.deliver, which sender never looks up
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so `send_with_retry` resolves `deliver` from the *sender* module globals at call time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the transport module attribute and leaves `notify.sender.deliver` pointing at the original function. This test therefore calls the real `deliver` three times — it will hit whatever the real transport does (network I/O, error, or an incidental falsy return), and it asserts nothing about the retry behaviour it claims to cover. If the real `deliver` happens to return falsy, the test passes for the wrong reason and will never catch a regression in the retry loop.

Patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, matching the existing test on line 2, and assert the call count is 3 so the "gives up after three failures" contract is actually verified.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry-exhaustion path is not actually tested

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`. Any field whose value contains a comma or a double quote (e.g. `{"a": "x,y"}`) produces a line with more fields than there are columns, silently corrupting the output and shifting every subsequent column for that row. The `csv_escape` helper added immediately below in the same commit does exactly this quoting but is never called. Wrap the field in it: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values, bypassing the csv_escape helper
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never routes values through `csv_escape`, which was added three lines below for exactly this purpose. Any record field that contains a comma splits into two columns, and a field containing a newline splits into two records, so whoever controls the content of a row (typically an end user whose name/description/notes field is being exported) can forge arbitrary additional columns or rows in the exported report — the downstream parser cannot tell the forged fields from real ones.

Fix: apply the escaper in the comprehension, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. While you are there, note that `csv_escape` only handles the delimiter/quote case; it does not neutralise a leading `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, so values reaching a spreadsheet are still exposed to formula injection. Prefixing such values with `'` (or using the stdlib `csv` module plus an explicit formula guard) closes both.

findings.title: csv_escape raises TypeError on non-string values
findings.body: The docstring says "Quote a value", but `"," in value` on line 12 requires a string; passing an int, `None`, or any non-string raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable`. Since row dictionaries in a reporting exporter will routinely hold numbers and `None`, coerce first (`value = str(value)` at the top of the function) or document that callers must stringify. This matters more once `csv_rows` starts calling it.

findings.title: New CSV export functions lack tests despite existing test pattern (and 2 more)
findings.body:
csv_rows and csv_escape are new public functions with no corresponding tests, even though the repo already has a test file (test_csv.py) covering csv_header in the same module. A bug in row rendering (e.g. wrong column order) or escaping (e.g. missing quote-wrapping) would go unnoticed.

The same gap appears at 2 other place(s) in this change:

- `reports/json_export.py:8` — New JSON export functions untested
- `reports/pdf_export.py:5` — New PDF layout functions untested

_Collapsed into one comment: this is one piece of work, not 3 separate ones._

findings.title: New test depends on wall-clock time, making it flaky and weak
findings.body:
Unlike test_token_expires_after_an_hour, which fixes both issued and now, test_token_issued_today_is_valid calls issue_token() and is_expired(token.expires_at) without an explicit 'now', so it depends on datetime.now(timezone.utc) at test-run time. The date() comparison on line 11 will intermittently fail if the test runs across a UTC midnight boundary, and because the token is issued and checked within the same instant, is_expired will pass trivially as long as the expiry window is not near-zero — it does not actually exercise the boundary condition the PR title claims to test ('the expiry window'). A real bug in the expiry threshold (e.g. off-by-a-day) could still pass this test as long as it runs well within the window.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test compares dates against the live clock and can flake at UTC midnight

findings.title: No test covers CouponExpired rejection path
findings.body: The PR's core behavior change—rejecting expired coupons by raising CouponExpired—has no test. The only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never exercises the new `if coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(...)` branch. If this comparison were inverted, always false, or the exception were never raised, no test would fail.

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires coupon.expires_at; old callers omit it
findings.body: `apply_coupon` unconditionally dereferences `coupon.expires_at`. The test change in this same PR shows that `Coupon(amount=10)` was previously a valid construction with no `expires_at`, so any caller or fixture that still builds a coupon that way now fails with `AttributeError` before reaching the discount logic. Either give `expires_at` a default on `Coupon` and treat the default (e.g. `None`) as "never expires", or guard the comparison: `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`. Please also confirm no production call site constructs coupons without the field.

findings.title: New CouponExpired branch has no test
findings.body: The only test exercises a coupon expiring tomorrow, so the new rejection path on lines 9–10 is never executed. Add a case asserting `pytest.raises(CouponExpired)` for a past `expires_at`, and ideally one at the exact boundary (`expires_at == now`) to pin down whether `<` or `<=` is intended — as written, a coupon expiring exactly now is still accepted.
